parameters.label: How blocked her nose is
parameters.explain: Chewing sends food smells up a channel at the back of the throat to the nose. A stuffed-up nose blocks that channel.

parameters.label: How strongly the food smells
parameters.explain: Strong-smelling foods send more aroma up to the nose, so they lose more flavour when the nose is blocked.

parameters.label: Sweetness of the food
parameters.explain: Sweet is one of the basic tastes the tongue picks up by itself — no nose needed.

parameters.label: Her usual sense of smell
parameters.explain: People's sense of smell differs a little, even when they're healthy.

explain.summary: Keisha's tongue can only pick up a few basic tastes, like sweet, sour and salty. Everything that makes strawberry taste like strawberry is a smell: when she chews, food smells travel up the back of her throat to her nose. Her cold has blocked that path, so the yogurt is just 'sweet' — until her nose clears.
rules: Flavour = the tongue's basic tastes + food smells reaching the nose.
The more blocked her nose, the less of the food's smell gets through.
Strong-smelling foods lose the most flavour when the nose is blocked.
Sweet, sour and salty come from the tongue, so they stay the same.

source.fact: Taste cells on the tongue respond to at least five basic tastes: sweet, sour, bitter, salty and umami.
Flavour is made when tastes combine with a food's aroma, which reaches the nose through a channel from the roof of the throat.
Without smell, foods tend to taste bland and have little flavour.
When a cold stuffs up the nose and blocks that channel, smells can't reach the smell cells; many people get their sense of smell back once they recover.

choice.what: Smell counts four times as much as the tongue in flavour
choice.why: Scientists agree most of flavour comes from smell but don't give one exact share; 4-to-1 shows 'most' clearly.

choice.what: Smell getting through falls in a straight line as the nose blocks
choice.why: Real noses don't block evenly, but a straight line keeps the idea simple.

choice.what: Aroma strength is shown in three steps
choice.why: Real foods vary continuously; three examples make the comparison easy.

illustrative: Keisha's 90%-blocked nose, the yogurt's sweetness and aroma, and her 'average' sense of smell are made up for a fictional story.
The 0–10 sweetness scale and the 'apple or potato' score are teaching scales.

citations.title: Taste Disorders
citations.supports: Taste cells respond to at least five basic tastes (sweet, sour, bitter, salty, umami); flavour forms when tastes combine with a food's aroma, which travels up a channel from the roof of the throat to the nose; a cold or flu that stuffs you up blocks it and you lose much of the enjoyment of flavour.

citations.title: Smell Disorders
citations.supports: Without smell, foods tend to taste bland; chewing releases aromas that reach the smell nerve cells through a channel from the roof of the throat to the nose; if it is blocked, as when stuffed up by a cold, smells can't get through; many people recover smell when the illness ends.

does: Shows flavour as basic tastes plus smell
Shows smell getting through less as the nose blocks
Shows the tongue's sweet taste staying the same
doesnt: Measure any real person's sense of smell or taste
Include texture, temperature, spiciness or bitter tastes
Explain long-lasting loss of smell, which has other causes
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: If you lose your sense of smell or taste for a long time without a stuffy nose, tell an adult.
